blocks.title: Phase
blocks.text: The angle theta = wt, which specifies both the displacement and the direction of motion of a point oscillating in S.H.M., is called its phase. Phase shows the state of motion of an oscillator.

In general the displacement is written x = xo cos(wt + phi) (14.18). The time-varying quantity (wt + phi) is the phase of the motion; it describes the state of motion at a given time. The constant phi is the phase constant (or phase angle); its value depends on the displacement and velocity of the particle at t = 0. The quantity phi also gives the phase difference between the states of motion of two oscillators.

items: phi = 0: x = xo cos(wt). At t = 0, T/2 and T (theta = 0, pi and 2 pi) the point is at an extreme position; at t = T/4 and 3T/4 (theta = pi/2 and 3 pi/2) it is at the mean position.

blocks.alt: Displacement against time over one period T, with T/4, T/2, 3T/4 and T marked and dashed lines at xo and -xo. The curve starts at +xo, crosses zero at T/4, reaches -xo at T/2, crosses zero at 3T/4 and is back at +xo at T.
blocks.caption: Figure 14.8 (a): Graph of x = xo cos(wt + phi) for phi = 0 degrees (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 14.8 (a)).

items: phi = 90 degrees: x = xo cos(wt + 90 degrees). At t = 0, T/2 and T the point is at the mean position; at T/4 and 3T/4 it is at an extreme.

blocks.alt: Displacement against time over one period. The curve starts at zero, falls to -xo at T/4, crosses zero at T/2, reaches +xo at 3T/4 and returns to zero at T.
blocks.caption: Figure 14.8 (b): Graph of x = xo cos(wt + phi) for phi = 90 degrees (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 14.8 (b)).

items: phi = 180 degrees: x = xo cos(wt + 180 degrees) = -xo cos(wt): the motion is the exact opposite of the first.

blocks.alt: Displacement against time over one period. The curve starts at -xo, crosses zero at T/4, reaches +xo at T/2, crosses zero at 3T/4 and is back at -xo at T: the mirror image of graph (a).
blocks.caption: Figure 14.8 (c): Graph of x = xo cos(wt + phi) for phi = 180 degrees (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 14.8 (c)).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed captions of Figure 14.8 give phi = 0 for (b) and phi = 90 degrees for (c); they are 90 and 180 degrees, as drawn above. Graph (c) also marks its lower level 'xo' where it is -xo.
When the phase difference between two oscillating systems is 180 degrees they are said to oscillate out of phase; when it is 0 or 360 degrees they oscillate in phase.

A 0.5 kg mass is attached to a spring with k = 200 N m^-1. It is displaced 0.2 m from equilibrium and released from rest. Assuming S.H.M., find its displacement, velocity and acceleration at t = 0.5 s. Solution: w = square root of (k/m) = square root of (200/0.5) = 20 rad s^-1, and since it starts from rest at the extreme, x = xo cos(wt). At t = 0.5 s, wt = 10 rad, and cos(10 rad) = -0.839, sin(10 rad) = -0.544. Displacement: x = 0.2 x (-0.839) = -0.168 m. Velocity: v = -xo w sin(wt) = -(0.2)(20)(-0.544) = +2.18 m s^-1. Acceleration: a = -w^2 x = -(400)(-0.168) = +67.1 m s^-2.
